name: Reminders That Work, and Reminders That Do Not
title: Reminders That Work, and Reminders That Do Not
answer: Reminders about college and financial aid steps work best when they come from someone the student knows, such as their own counselor, rather than from a large outside campaign. Large scale alone does not move students to act, so messages need a relationship behind them and a clear next step for that particular student. AI can help counselors send these personal reminders to many students at once, while the counselor keeps the relationship.

sections.body: This idea is about who sends a reminder and what it says, because those two things decide whether a student acts. Several large trials found that the source of a message matters more than its reach, and that campaigns sent from outside organizations often changed nothing. The problem it solves is wasted effort, where schools and programs spend heavily on broad messaging that students ignore. The answer is to send reminders through a relationship the student already has, and to make each message about that student's own next step. AI makes this possible at a scale a counselor could not manage by hand.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a counselor drafts messages about upcoming deadlines and uses the school's texting platform to send them to the right students. Each message names the student's actual next step, such as submitting a transcript or finishing a financial aid form, and it carries the counselor's name and a way to reply so it stays personal. Deadline tracking tools such as Scoir and BigFuture let students follow their own applications and deadlines, and let a counselor see who is behind and reach out. The tool keeps the list, and the counselor keeps the relationship. The text does not give grade bands for this practice.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with several large trials. In Texas, text messages from students' own counselors raised college steps and enrollment for some groups of students (Avery et al., 2021), while a national campaign sending similar messages from an outside organization had mostly no effect. Two trials of national and state financial aid campaigns reached about 800,000 students and found no effect on aid or enrollment (Bird et al., 2021). A national trial with 785,000 students tested brochures, emails, texts, and application fee waivers to encourage enrollment at selective colleges, and it too found no change (Gurantz et al., 2020). The finding is that scale alone does not produce results, and messages must reach students through a relationship and address their specific situation.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about who the message comes from and what it asks. An outside organization sending similar messages mostly had no effect, so a school cannot hand the relationship to a platform and expect the same result. The message has to name the student's real next step, which means someone has to know that step, and the counselor's name and a reply path keep it personal. The tool keeps the list, and the counselor keeps the relationship, so the judgment about which students are behind and what to say stays with a person. Nothing in the text sets out legal duties, and this is a description of practice rather than legal advice.
